posts.title: 2026.47: Down in DC
posts.summary: The best Stratechery content from the week of November 16, 2026, including obituaries and exceptionalism, arguments about agents, and Ben gets a Duo.
bullets: The departure of Jensen Huang marks a significant inflection point for the tech industry, signaling the end of an era defined by his specific leadership and strategic vision.
U.S. government policy toward AI and large tech companies is undergoing a fundamental shift, creating a regulatory environment that Huang struggled to navigate effectively.

Data from OpenRouter indicates that the AI market is not consolidating as expected; the median number of model families used by high-spending customers has doubled from three to six over the past year.
Expert debate persists regarding the viability of agentic commerce, with conflicting views on whether current hype reflects genuine technological utility or market over-optimism.

posts.title: Chip Industry Week In Review
posts.summary:
Intel's first 18A-P external customer; Siemens buys Breker; backside clock distribution; Microsoft taps EMIB; export controls tighten around China; Nvidia expands packaging capacity; SC26 brings new HPC HW; JEDEC previews DDR6; Europe pushes ahead with €33B in chip projects.
The post Chip Industry Week In Review appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: Intel Foundry secured its first external customer for the 18A-P process and expanded its partnership with Microsoft, which will utilize Intel's EMIB packaging for custom Azure silicon.
Siemens is set to acquire Breker Verification Systems to bolster its AI-driven verification capabilities, while AMD continues its aggressive AI expansion by acquiring Taalas and World Labs.
The EU Chips Act has now approved over 20 projects totaling more than €33 billion in investment, signaling a significant acceleration in regional semiconductor manufacturing capacity.

New U.S. export controls have expanded to cover remote access to AI computing and added licensing requirements for several nations, while government data reveals that only about 25% of requested AI chip licenses for China were approved.
GlobalFoundries is scaling its robotics integration by deploying Boston Dynamics' Spot robots across global fabs, with plans to test humanoid Atlas robots for manufacturing tasks by 2027.

posts.title: The FDIB Strategy: A New Geography of American Industrial Power
posts.summary:
In April, Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg previewed an ambitious economic initiative that has been termed the “Forward Deployed Industrial Base” (FDIB). The United States is negotiating with the Philippines to secure a four-thousand-acre, rent-free lease on the island of Luzon. Using primarily American private capital, the State Department intends to…

bullets: The State Department is developing the 'Forward Deployed Industrial Base' (FDIB) strategy, starting with a 4,000-acre, rent-free zone in the Philippines to host AI, semiconductor, and critical mineral infrastructure.
The initiative aims to create a 'constellation' of such zones globally, utilizing private capital to secure supply chains outside of traditional domestic or hostile-adjacent territories.

The strategy raises complex legal questions, with the author advocating for the application of American common law and dispute resolution mechanisms within these zones to ensure operational stability.

posts.title: Why America’s Chip Controls Are No Longer Sufficient
posts.summary:
Since 2022, the United States has used export controls on advanced chips and manufacturing equipment to slow China’s progress in artificial intelligence. The underlying assumption was that frontier AI depends on access to massive amounts of high-performance compute, including sufficiently advanced chips. By this logic, the United States could preserve a durable lead in a…
Continue reading Why America’s Chip Controls Are No Longer Sufficient on American Affairs Journal.
bullets: The release of Moonshot AI’s 2.8-trillion-parameter Kimi K3 model demonstrates that Chinese firms can achieve frontier-class AI performance despite long-standing U.S. semiconductor export controls.
The proliferation of high-performance, open-weight models suggests that export controls on hardware are increasingly insufficient to maintain a durable lead in AI capabilities.
The U.S. market is shifting toward a focus on commercial adoption and cost-efficiency, as the diffusion of advanced AI capabilities renders hardware-centric containment strategies less effective.

posts.title: Varieties of Financial Statecraft: Sanctions and Sovereign Reserves After Ukraine
posts.summary:
The futures of both American economic power and the achievement of foreign policy goals depend on a good understanding of that tension. Even a settlement in Ukraine would not fully restore the pre-2022 assumption that sovereign reserves are untouchable, and that altered assumption is the lasting consequence of this case. The resulting loss of confidence in the global economy due to the uncertainty of investment has already taken effect. The questions facing Washington (and Brussels) are not only how and to what extent sanctions can be made to work, but also how much of the global financial system that enforces those sanctions they are willing to see reshaped in the process.
Continue reading Varieties of Financial Statecraft: Sanctions and Sovereign Reserves After Ukraine on American Affairs Journal.
bullets: The 2022 'shock and awe' sanctions on Russia, including the freezing of $300 billion in sovereign reserves, failed to trigger the expected economic collapse of the Russian state.
Russia’s economy demonstrated unexpected resilience, growing by 8.7 percent in real terms between 2021 and 2025 despite the unprecedented financial isolation.
The reliance on dollar- and euro-denominated assets for reserves has proven to be a strategic liability, prompting other nations to reconsider their custody strategies to avoid similar vulnerability.
